abstract: This study uses a large-scale randomized controlled experiment during the 2020 US presidential election to test how removing reshared content from Facebook feeds affects users' political attitudes, knowledge, and behavior. Consenting US-based users were randomly assigned to a 'No Reshares' condition (feeds stripped of reshared posts) or a control condition for roughly three months. Removing reshares substantially changed the mix and volume of content users saw—cutting political news, untrustworthy-source content, and engagement—but did not produce detectable effects on political polarization or nearly any measure of political attitudes, with only mixed evidence for reduced news knowledge.
key_claims: Reshares are a core amplification mechanism on Facebook that substantially shape the content users encounter, especially political news and content from untrustworthy sources.
Removing reshared content decreases exposure to political news, untrustworthy-source content, and overall engagement (clicks and reactions), and reduces clicks on partisan news.

Despite altering the content environment, suppressing reshares does not detectably affect political polarization (affective or issue) or almost any individual-level political attitude or offline behavior.
There is suggestive but uncertain evidence that removing reshares reduces news knowledge within the sample, though this may not generalize to the full user population.
Reshares can act as a 'double-edged sword,' promoting exposure to both reliable news and lower-quality/untrustworthy content, yet with limited downstream attitudinal impact.
methods: Randomized controlled experiment embedded in the 2020 US Facebook and Instagram Election Study (FIES), with participants recruited via feed survey invitations seen by ~14.6 million users; N=193,880 consented.

Two experimental conditions analyzed: a control group with unchanged feeds and a 'No Reshares' treatment group whose feeds excluded reshared content from friends, Groups, and Pages, active 24 September–23 December 2020.
Analytic samples of N=23,402 for survey data and N=3,781 for passive web-tracking data (participants completing the first two surveys plus at least one of three later waves).

Preregistered design, measures, and analysis (OSF); primary estimand is the population average treatment effect (PATE) weighted by predicted ideology, friend count, political pages followed, and activity, with unweighted sample average treatment effect (SATE) also reported.

Outcomes measured via five surveys, Facebook platform behavioral data, and web-visit tracking; content classified for political relevance, news, untrustworthy sources, incivility, slurs, and like-minded/cross-cutting/moderate ideological alignment.

Covariate-adjusted OLS regression with HC2 robust standard errors; multiple-comparison correction via sharpened false discovery rate (FDR) adjustment; assessment of attrition and treatment effect heterogeneity.
findings: Reshared content fell from 28% of views in control to 5.8% in the No Reshares group; political content dropped from 13.5% to 10.8%, political news from 6.2% to 2.5%, and untrustworthy-source content from 2.6% to 1.8%.
Uncivil content rose slightly (3.2% to 3.4%) and moderate/mixed-source content rose ~16%, while both like-minded and cross-cutting content decreased modestly; slur exposure was unaffected.

Treatment reduced daily time on Facebook, click rate (8.3% to 7.5%), and reaction rate, but did not change users' own reshares, likes, or comments; content from friends fell ~10 points while Groups (+8) and Pages (+2) rose.

No significant effects on affective or issue polarization (FDR-adjusted p>0.8), nor on trust in media, institutional confidence, election legitimacy beliefs, factual accuracy perceptions, or support for political violence, after multiple-comparison correction.

News knowledge fell significantly in the sample (SATE −0.069 SD, p<0.01) but the PATE (−0.053 SD) fell short of significance after FDR adjustment (p=0.16); election knowledge showed no distinguishable effect.
The one robust behavioral effect was a decrease in clicks on partisan news content (PATE −0.109 SD, p<0.01); off-platform political news visits were unaffected.
Exploratory analyses found a 62% decrease in mainstream news exposure in the treatment group as a possible contributor to knowledge effects, while ruling out several other mechanisms.
contributions: Provides rigorous, large-scale experimental (rather than correlational) evidence on the causal effects of a specific platform feature—resharing—during a real election.

Demonstrates that a widely proposed platform intervention (removing reshares) meaningfully changes content exposure and on-platform behavior but has limited detectable impact on political attitudes and offline behaviors.
Quantifies the composition of reshared content and its role in amplifying political news and untrustworthy sources, clarifying that most reshared content does not go viral.
Offers precise null and near-null estimates with power to rule out even moderately sized effects, informing debates on social media's political influence.
Contributes preregistered design, transparent PATE/SATE reporting, and archived data/code as a model for industry-academic collaborative research.
framing: The paper situates itself in research on social media's role in political polarization, misinformation, and incidental learning, engaging debates over whether virality-enabling features amplify harmful political effects. It builds on prior experimental work (e.g., Facebook deactivation studies) and policy proposals to limit resharing, testing whether a hypothesized amplification mechanism translates into measurable attitudinal change.
